lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Mauricio | Lesson 8 -- Twelve Minutes

listenings.text: Let me summarize before I start, so you know where this is going. We closed a site, it went badly, and the reason was not the one we wrote in the report. Now the story. Initially we were running four sites and losing money on one of them for about three years. At that point a new finance director arrived and asked why. Nobody had a good answer. Our analysis showed the site was not the problem; the contract behind it was. As a result, we closed the site anyway, because closing was easier to explain than renegotiating. The impact was two hundred jobs and a supply gap we are still fixing. In the end, the root cause was that we optimised for the easy conversation. My recommendation is simple: when the analysis and the decision disagree, write down why. Happy to take questions.

A word on Wednesday, because people worry about the wrong things. Nobody is counting your slides and nobody cares about your accent. Three things decide whether a case lands. First: do we know, in the first thirty seconds, what happened and why it matters. Second: is there one number we remember. Third: does the recommendation follow from the analysis, or did you decide first and analyse afterwards. That third one is where most cases fall apart, including some very polished ones. And please leave four minutes for questions. A case with no questions at the end is not a compliment.
